summary: Defines an extensible message format for responses to message tracking requests. Tracking is used along with delivery status and message disposition notifications, usually when one of them has not arrived in a reasonable time.

plainLanguage.summary: When a sender asks where a message has got to, the mail servers answer with a report in a fixed format. This RFC defines that format as a MIME type called message/tracking-status, with one block of fields for the message as a whole and one block for each recipient. The Action field in each recipient block says whether the message failed, is waiting, was delivered or was passed on, and whether the requester should keep asking further servers.

questions: what do the tracking action values mean
subtitle: The MIME format a mail server uses to report where a tracked message currently is.

tldr.problem: When a sender asks where a message has got to, the answer needs a standard, machine-readable form that works across servers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the message/tracking-status MIME type, modelled on the delivery status format of RFC 3464, with per-message fields followed by groups of per-recipient fields, including an Action field with seven values.
tldr.outcome: Servers can report whether a message failed, is queued, was delivered, expanded, relayed, transferred or is opaque, and tracking agents know when to keep asking further downstream. The RFC updates RFC 3463 with one status code.

facts.label: Action values
facts.value: 7: failed, delayed, delivered, expanded, relayed, transferred, opaque

facts.label: New status code
facts.value: X.1.9, message relayed to non-compliant mailer

today: RFC 3886 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3463 by adding one status code, X.1.9, for a message relayed to a non-compliant mailer.

sections.title: What This Memo Does and Does Not Define
sections.content:
Message Tracking is expected to be used to determine the status of undelivered e-mail upon request. Tracking is used in conjunction with Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs) and Message Disposition Notifications (MDNs). Generally, a message tracking request will be issued only when a DSN or MDN has not been received within a reasonable timeout period.

This memo defines a MIME content-type for message tracking status in the same spirit as RFC 3464, 'An Extensible Message Format for Delivery Status Notifications'. It is to be issued upon a request as described in the Message Tracking Query Protocol. This memo defines only the format of the status information: the extension to SMTP that labels messages for further tracking and requests tracking status is defined in a separate memo, RFC 3885.

Message tracking is intended for use as a last resort mechanism. Normally, Delivery Status Notifications and Message Disposition Notifications would provide the primary delivery status, and only if no response is received from either of those mechanisms would Message Tracking be used. The model used for Message Tracking is described in RFC 3888.
sections.plainLanguage: Tracking is used to find out what happened to a message that was never confirmed. Delivery status notifications and message disposition notifications normally report the outcome, so tracking is only asked for when neither arrives in time. This RFC defines the shape of the answer, not how the question is sent.

sections.title: The Format of a Tracking Status Report
sections.content:
A Message Tracking Status Notification (MTSN) is intended to be returned as the body of a Message Tracking request. The actual body MUST be a multipart/related with type parameter of message/tracking-status, and each subpart MUST be of type message/tracking-status. The multipart/related body can include multiple message/tracking-status parts if an MTQP server chains requests to the next server.

The content type has MIME type name message, MIME subtype name tracking-status and no optional parameters. The 7bit encoding is sufficient and MUST be used to maintain readability when viewed by non-MIME mail readers.

The body of a message/tracking-status is modelled after RFC 3464. It consists of one or more fields formatted according to the ABNF of RFC 2822 header fields. The per-message fields appear first, followed by a blank line, and then one or more groups of per-recipient fields, each group preceded by a blank line. There is a blank line between the final per-recipient field and the MIME boundary, since one CRLF terminates the field and a second introduces the boundary.

tracking-status-content =
          per-message-fields 1*( CRLF per-recipient-fields )
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a MIME multipart/related body whose parts are of type message/tracking-status. It uses 7bit encoding so it stays readable in mail readers that do not understand MIME. The body holds one set of fields about the whole message, then a blank line, then one group of fields for each recipient, with a blank line before each group.

sections.title: The Fields About the Whole Message
sections.content:
Some fields of an MTSN apply to all of the addresses in a single envelope. These fields may appear at most once in any MTSN. They are used to correlate the MTSN with the original message transaction and to provide additional information which may be useful to gateways.

per-message-fields =
          original-envelope-id-field CRLF
          reporting-mta-field CRLF
          arrival-date-field CRLF
          *( extension-field CRLF )

Three fields are REQUIRED. The Original-Envelope-Id field is defined as in section 2.2.1 of RFC 3464. The Reporting-MTA field is defined as in section 2.2.2 of RFC 3464. The Arrival-Date field is defined as in section 2.2.5 of RFC 3464. Any number of extension fields may follow them.
sections.plainLanguage: The three fields at the top are required. Original-Envelope-Id ties the answer to the envelope the message was sent in. Reporting-MTA names the server that is answering. Arrival-Date says when the message arrived. Any number of extension fields can follow.

sections.title: The Fields About Each Recipient
sections.content:
An MTSN contains information about attempts to deliver a message to one or more recipients. The delivery information for any particular recipient is contained in a group of contiguous per-recipient fields.

per-recipient-fields =
          original-recipient-field CRLF
          final-recipient-field CRLF
          action-field CRLF
          status-field CRLF
          [ remote-mta-field CRLF ]
          [ last-attempt-date-field CRLF ]
          [ will-retry-until-field CRLF ]
          *( extension-field CRLF )

The Original-Recipient and Final-Recipient fields are REQUIRED. The Action field is REQUIRED and MUST be present for each recipient named in the MTSN. The Status field is REQUIRED. The three optional fields have extra rules.

  • Remote-MTA MUST NOT be included if no delivery attempts have been made or if the Action field has value opaque. If delivery went to an agent other than an MTA, such as a Local Delivery Agent, the field MAY be included, giving the name of the host on which that agent was contacted.
  • Last-Attempt-Date is REQUIRED if any delivery attempt has been made and the Action field does not have value opaque, and MUST NOT be included if no delivery attempts have been made.
  • Will-Retry-Until MUST NOT be included if the message is not in the local queue or the Action field has the value opaque; otherwise the field SHOULD be included.

The Status field is defined as in RFC 3464, with one new code added to RFC 3463: X.1.9, message relayed to non-compliant mailer, meaning that the mailbox address specified was valid but the message has been relayed to a system that does not speak this protocol. A 2.1.9 Status field MUST be used exclusively with a relayed Action field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each recipient has four required fields: who the address was, who it became, what the server did, and the status code. Three more fields are optional and have rules. Remote-MTA names the host contacted and must be left out if no attempt was made. Last-Attempt-Date is required once an attempt has been made. Will-Retry-Until must be left out when the message is not in the queue.

sections.title: The Seven Action Values
sections.content:
The Action field indicates the action performed by the Reporting-MTA as a result of its attempt to deliver the message to this recipient address. The valid actions are:

  • failed: the message could not be delivered. If DSNs have been enabled, a failed DSN should already have been returned.
  • delayed: the message is currently waiting in the MTA queue for future delivery. Essentially, this action means the message is located and it is here.
  • delivered: the message has been successfully delivered to the final recipient, including delivery to a mailing list exploder. It does not indicate that the message has been read, and the tracking agent SHOULD NOT attempt further downstream tracking requests.
  • expanded: the message has been successfully delivered to the recipient address as specified by the sender and forwarded by the Reporting-MTA beyond that destination to multiple additional recipient addresses. Those additional addresses are not trackable, and the tracking agent SHOULD NOT attempt further downstream tracking requests.
  • relayed: the message has been delivered into an environment that does not support message tracking. No further information is available, and the tracking agent SHOULD NOT attempt further downstream tracking requests.
  • transferred: the message has been transferred to another MTRK-compliant MTA. The tracking agent SHOULD attempt further downstream tracking requests unless that information is already given in a chaining response.
  • opaque: the message may or may not have been seen by this system. No further information is available or forthcoming.

There may be some confusion between when to use expanded and when to use delivered. Whenever possible, expanded should be used when the MTA knows that the message will be sent to multiple addresses. However, in some cases the delivery occurs to a program which, unknown to the MTA, causes mailing list expansion. If the MTA cannot ensure that the delivery will cause list expansion, it should set the action to delivered.

A message delivered to a Local Delivery Agent that understands message tracking, in particular an LDA speaking LMTP that supports the MTRK extension, SHOULD pass the tracking request to the LDA. In that case the Action field for the MTA to LDA exchange looks the same as a transfer to a compliant MTA, so a transferred tracking status is issued.
sections.plainLanguage: The Action field has seven possible values. Some mean the tracking stops there, because the message reached its destination or left the tracking system. One value, transferred, means another server that understands tracking has the message, so the requester should keep asking further servers. The RFC also says when to choose expanded over delivered, and how to report a handoff to a local delivery agent.

sections.title: Forgery, Confidentiality and Mailing Lists
sections.content:
Malicious servers may attempt to subvert message tracking and return false information. This could result in misdirection or misinterpretation of results.

Confidentiality is another dimension of security. There may be cases in which a message recipient is autoforwarding messages but does not wish to divulge the address to which the messages are autoforwarded. The desire for such confidentiality will probably be heightened as wireless mailboxes, such as pagers, become more widely used as autoforward addresses. MTA authors are encouraged to provide a mechanism which enables the end user to preserve the confidentiality of a forwarding address. Depending on the degree of confidentiality required and the nature of the environment, this might be accomplished by responding with a relayed tracking status when a message is forwarded to a confidential forwarding address and disabling further message tracking requests, or by declaring the message to be delivered, issuing a delivered tracking status, re-sending the message to the confidential forwarding address, and disabling further message tracking requests.

The tracking algorithms MUST NOT allow tracking through list expansions. When a message is delivered to a list, a tracking request MUST respond with an expanded tracking status and MUST NOT display the contents of the list.
sections.plainLanguage: A server could lie about where a message is, so the answer has to be treated with care. Some recipients forward mail to a private address and do not want that address revealed, so the format can stop the trail there. Tracking through a mailing list is not allowed: the answer must say expanded and must not show the list.

viz.caption: THE GRAMMAR OF A TRACKING STATUS BODY

data.title: tracking-status-content
data.code:
tracking-status-content =
          per-message-fields 1*( CRLF per-recipient-fields )

per-message-fields =
          original-envelope-id-field CRLF
          reporting-mta-field CRLF
          arrival-date-field CRLF
          *( extension-field CRLF )

per-recipient-fields =
          original-recipient-field CRLF
          final-recipient-field CRLF
          action-field CRLF
          status-field CRLF
          [ remote-mta-field CRLF ]
          [ last-attempt-date-field CRLF ]
          [ will-retry-until-field CRLF ]
          *( extension-field CRLF )

items.label: Not delivered
items.desc: The message could not be delivered.

items.label: Waiting in the queue
items.desc: The message is waiting in the MTA queue for future delivery.

items.label: Delivered
items.desc: Delivered to the final recipient. It does not mean the message was read.

items.label: Delivered to many
items.desc: Delivered to the address given, then forwarded to more addresses that are not trackable.

items.label: Left the tracking system
items.desc: Delivered into an environment that does not support message tracking.

items.label: Unknown
items.desc: The message may or may not have been seen by this system.
